title: The lord and the servant (Revelations 51)
hook: a servant falls in a ditch rushing to serve, and the lord looks on him only with love
tomorrow: why would Julian call Jesus our mother?

segments.voice: The ground of our asking: God wills it, stirs the wanting, and then we ask. He wants you to ask. Next, Julian is shown a story, and puzzles over it for a long time.
screen: `HE WANTS YOU TO ASK.` → `A STORY SHE PUZZLED OVER.`

segments.voice: Rushing to help is its own kind of accident. Someone grabs the grocery bags to save a trip, and the eggs hit the driveway. Someone hits reply-all to fix a mistake and makes a bigger one. Julian of Norwich was shown a scene like that, in chapter fifty-one of her book. A lord sits in rest and peace. A servant stands ready. The lord sends him on an errand, and the servant doesn't just go. He leaps up and runs, in great haste, for love. And almost at once he falls into a ditch, and he's badly hurt.
screen: `THE EGGS HIT THE DRIVEWAY.` → `HE RUNS, FOR LOVE.` → `INTO THE DITCH.`

segments.voice: Julian watches him lying there. He groans and twists, and he can't get up. And the worst hurt, she says, isn't the fall. It's that he can't turn his face to see his lord, who is right beside him and loves him. So he feels alone. And the lord? Julian looks carefully for any blame in him, and finds none. The lord looks on him with tenderness and pity. See my beloved servant, the lord says, what harm and hurt he has taken in my service, for my love, and for his good will. Isn't it right that I reward him? Julian says she didn't understand this showing at first, and carried it with her for years. Then she came to see the servant as Adam, which is to say every one of us. We fall rushing toward good things; the fall hurts; and what hurts most is losing sight of the face still turned toward us. And she saw a second meaning laid over the first: the servant is also Christ, who came down into the ditch with us. In Paul's words, he "took upon him the form of a servant." Here's the one to tell a friend: the story doesn't pretend the fall doesn't matter. The servant is really hurt. But the lord's look never changes.
screen: `HE CAN'T TURN HIS FACE.` · `NO BLAME IN THE LORD.` · `THE SERVANT IS ADAM: ALL OF US.` · `AND THE SERVANT IS CHRIST.` · then, large: `HE FELL RUSHING TO SERVE.`

segments.voice: On paper, write one line about a recent fall: something that went wrong while you were trying, maybe too fast, to do right. Beside it, write the verdict Julian's lord gives: he fell rushing to serve. Then sit, and look at the page with pity and no blame.
The lord and the servant. Julian's parable of a servant who falls in his eagerness, and a lord who looks on him only with love.
screen: `THE LORD AND THE SERVANT — today's word`.

segments.voice: The line for today: he fell rushing to serve, and the lord's look never changed. See you tomorrow.
